diagnosis.report:
**Why api is down:** the database port is set to `abc` instead of a number, so the app quits within a second of starting, every time.

The container's startup script prints the database address and then checks that `DB_PORT` is a number. The single pod's log shows that check failing:

[[radar:evidence=0]]

`DB_PORT` comes from the ConfigMap `app-config` (a small key/value config object the Deployment loads as environment variables), and its live value is literally `abc`:

[[radar:evidence=1]]

Other causes don't fit. The image runs fine: the script gets far enough to print its own error. Memory is tiny and the exit is a plain error code 1, not an out-of-memory kill. The restart count rises at a flat rate of about 12 an hour for the whole 7-day metrics window. That points to a value that has been wrong for at least that long, not something that broke recently:

[[radar:evidence=2|compact]]

Radar's change history only reaches back to late on 2026-10-27, so I can't tell whether `abc` was there since 2026-10-17, when the ConfigMap and Deployment were created together, or was edited in later. That doesn't change the fix.

**The fix:** put the real numeric port into `app-config`, then restart the Deployment. Environment variables from a ConfigMap are read only when the container starts, so the edit alone won't take effect. I haven't recommended a one-click fix because nothing I read shows the correct port. If the database is Postgres, 5432 is a plausible guess, but confirm it first. Also correct the source this ConfigMap is deployed from, or the next deploy will bring `abc` back.

ruledOut.hypothesis: The container is being OOM-killed or starved of resources

diagnosis.report:
The error message points the wrong way. "Queue credentials rejected" sounds like an authentication failure, but no queue is involved. The Deployment's container is a plain busybox image whose command is a one-line shell script: print that sentence, then `exit 1`. Nothing in it connects to anything, and it references no Secret, ConfigMap or environment variable that could hold credentials.

[[radar:evidence=0]]

Every start therefore ends the same way. The last run lived 0 seconds, logged the hard-coded line and exited with code 1.

[[radar:evidence=1|compact]]

`generation: 1` shows the spec has not been edited since the Deployment was created on 2026-10-17, so no recent change broke it. Prometheus shows a steady ~12 restarts per hour from 2026-10-23 onward, the earliest data it holds. At that rate the 1698 restarts already counted on 2026-10-23 work out to roughly six days of crashing, consistent with a crash loop dating from creation. That is an extrapolation, though; the metrics do not cover those first days.

[[radar:evidence=2|compact]]

Rotating credentials or adding memory will not help. The fix is to replace the placeholder command with the real worker image and entrypoint. I couldn't find what those should be: Radar sees no Helm, Argo CD or Flux owner, so the owner of the source manifest has to supply them. Until then, scaling to zero stops the restart churn without losing any work. The privilege-escalation and token-mounting audit findings are worth fixing later but have nothing to do with this crash.

A recent spec or config edit broke the worker
Container is OOM-killed or starved by resource limits

diagnosis.report:
Kubernetes can't start the checkout container, and it has failed this way since the Deployment was created on 2026-10-17. The pod template pulls all its environment variables from a ConfigMap named `checkout-settings`, and that reference is required, not optional. That ConfigMap does not exist. Before starting the container, the kubelet (the node agent that runs pods) tries to read it, fails, and parks the pod in `CreateContainerConfigError`. It has retried 66,566 times.

[[radar:evidence=0]]

The Deployment is still at its first revision with an unedited spec, and it has been unavailable since the minute it was created. So this isn't a recent break. The pod has not started since creation. The only ConfigMaps in the namespace are the automatically injected Kubernetes and Istio CA certificates, so there is nothing misspelled or renamed to point at.

[[radar:evidence=2]]

Radar's change history only goes back to 2026-10-27, so it can't show whether `checkout-settings` was ever applied and then removed. That doesn't change the fix.

Why I haven't picked a one-click fix: creating an empty ConfigMap or marking the reference optional would let the pod start, but possibly without the settings checkout actually needs. Nothing I could read shows what keys belong in it. Get the real contents from wherever the app's manifests live, create the ConfigMap (step 2), and the stuck pod will start on its next retry without a restart. Use the optional-reference patch only if the app owner confirms the settings aren't needed.

The privilege-escalation and token-automount audit findings are general security hygiene and have nothing to do with this outage.

diagnosis.report:
adservice is healthy. Radar's green status matches what the cluster shows. The deployment has its one replica ready and available, and Kubernetes has reported it available continuously since 2026-10-23 23:30 UTC.

[[radar:evidence=0|compact]]

The pod is doing its job. Its most recent log lines are routine "received ad request" entries from seconds before this check, with no errors or stack traces. It is nowhere near its limits: memory sits flat at about 106 MB under a 300 MiB cap, and CPU is close to idle.

[[radar:evidence=2]]

The pod has not restarted at any point in the last seven days, and Kubernetes holds no earlier crashed container for it. So there is no hidden crash loop or out-of-memory kill behind the green status.

The two audit findings are configuration hygiene, not live faults. One is that the pod gets a Kubernetes API token it probably doesn't need. The other is that the deployment was applied by hand rather than from Git or Helm. Neither affects the service today.

These checks would not catch errors seen only by the callers, such as the frontend timing out on ad requests. If someone reports missing ads, look at the frontend's logs next.
